e-4716.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

The given matrix $E$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2:= R_2+(-5) R_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Find the inverse of the elementary matrix

e-4718.worked_solution:
We write down $E$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=\frac{5}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,

An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only W and Z are elementary matrices.

after.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrices $P$ and $Q$ are not elementary matrices because they can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $S$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =S\end{aligned}

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrices $A$ and $C$ are not elementary matrices because they can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:=4{R}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:=4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $B$ is an elementary matrix.

decision.explanation: K adds 8 times the first row to the second row. Its inverse undoes this with R₂ ← R₂ − 8R₁, giving the matrix with −8 in the lower-left entry. Multiplying it by K gives I₂.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$K=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-8){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -8 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

a

EXPLANATION

We write down K and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[K|I]=[10108101]R2:=R2+(−8)R1∼[101001−81]

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,

K−1=[10−81].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$K=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
We write down $K$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[K\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-8){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -8 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We write down $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$

We write down A and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
We write down $A$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{A}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: The inverse undoes scaling the first row by −3/2 by scaling it by −2/3. Since (−3/2)(−2/3) = 1, the resulting product is I₂.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$G=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We write down $G$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[G\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:=-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{G}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

We write down G and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[G|I]=[−320100101]R1:=−23R1∼[10−2300101]

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,

G−1=[−23001].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$G=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
content.worked_solution:
We write down $G$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[G\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:=-\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{G}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We write down $Q$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[Q\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{7} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+\frac{1}{7}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{Q}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: B subtracts 10 times the first row from the second. Its inverse adds 10 times the first row to the second, giving lower-left entry 10. The product is I₂ because −10 + 10 = 0.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -10 & 1\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We write down $B$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[B\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -10 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+10{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 10 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{B}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 10 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

We write down B and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[B|I]=[1010−10101]R2:=R2+10R1∼[101001101]

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, B−1=[10101].

decision.explanation: E₂⁻¹ has diagonal entries 1 and −2. Multiplying E₁ by E₂⁻¹ gives entries 1, 0, −2, −2: the lower-left entry is (−2)(1)+(1)(0)=−2, and the lower-right entry is (−2)(0)+(1)(−2)=−2.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 11
?

Find the product E1E2−1, where E1=[10−21],E2=[100−12].

a
[1024−2]
b
[10−2−2]
c
[10242]
d
[10−4−2]
e
[1−2−4−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that E1 and E2 are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find E2−1. We write down E2 and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[E2|I]=[10100−1201]R2:=(−2)R2∼[1010010−2]

Therefore,

E2−1=[100−2].

Now, we can find the product E1E2−1:

E1E2−1=[10−21][100−2]=[10−2−2]

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Product Involving the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$

Find the product E1E2−1, where E1=[3001],E2=[1201].

[−6301]

[3−601]

EXPLANATION

Notice that E1 and E2 are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find E2−1. We write down E2 and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[E2|I]=[12100101]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[101−20101]

Therefore,

E2−1=[1−201].

Now, we can find the product E1E2−1:

E1E2−1=[3001][1−201]=[3−601]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c. E₂⁻¹ has first row [1, −2] and second row [0, 1]. Multiplying on the left by E₁ scales the first row by 3, producing [3, −6] and [0, 1].

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Product Involving the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}21 & -4 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: E₂⁻¹ has lower-left entry −1 and diagonal entries 1. In E₁E₂⁻¹, the lower-left entry is (−6)(1)+(1)(−1)=−7; the other entries are 1, 0, and 1.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -7 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -6 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -7 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: E₂⁻¹ has diagonal entries 1 and −4. Multiplying E₁ by E₂⁻¹ leaves its first column unchanged and multiplies its second column by −4, giving rows [1, 0] and [3, −4].

after.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 15

Find the product E1E2−1, where E1=[1031],E2=[100−14].

a
[103−4]
b
[103−1]
c
[104−3]
d
[130−4]
e
[−4031]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that E1 and E2 are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find E2−1. We write down E2 and the identity matrix I side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

[E2|I]=[10100−1401]R2:=(−4)R2∼[1010010−4]

Therefore,

E2−1=[100−4].

Now, we can find the product E1E2−1:

E1E2−1=[1031][100−4]=[103−4]

content.knowledge_point: Computing a Product Involving the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$
